items.text: Autistic burnout isn't depression. It has its own definition: chronic exhaustion, loss of skills, sharply reduced tolerance. They don't respond to the same treatment. That distinction isn't minor.
items.rationale: Names the clinical distinction precisely without prescribing anything — validates years of 'treatment-resistant' experiences by pointing at the wrong frame, not the person.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'They don't respond to the same treatment' edges toward treatment guidance. Defensible from Raymaker et al. but recommend editorial sign-off before posting.

items.text: Years of anxiety and depression diagnoses that never quite fit. For many late-diagnosed autistic people, what was actually happening was burnout — a nervous system mismatch with a world not built for them.
items.rationale: Mirrors the exact narrative late-diagnosed autistic people tell about their diagnostic history. Recognition-heavy without medicalizing or advising.

items.text: AuDHD isn't autism stacked on top of ADHD. It's more like tie-dye — the two blend into something with its own patterns that neither label fully predicts.
items.rationale: The tie-dye metaphor is memorable and accurate — it replaces a clunky additive model with something that matches lived experience. Short enough to share intact.

items.text: 70% of neurodivergent employees don't know what workplace accommodations they can request. 56% of those who got them say it improved their experience. The gap isn't ambition. It's information.
items.rationale: Leading with the stat makes the information gap concrete and systemic. The closing line reframes struggling at work as an information problem, not a personal failure.

items.text: If you've been struggling at work and telling yourself you just need to try harder — 70% of neurodivergent employees don't even know what accommodations they can request. That's not a character issue.
items.rationale: Addresses imposter syndrome directly by naming the 'just try harder' internal monologue before delivering the stat. Meets people where they already are.

items.text: 'Pathological Demand Avoidance' → 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy.' The debate isn't settled — PDA isn't in the DSM or ICD. But the direction matters: one treats a need as a flaw. The other doesn't.
items.rationale: Acknowledges the live clinical dispute honestly — PDA outside DSM/ICD — while still landing the core reframe. Gives both sides of the community something genuine to respond to.
items.sensitivity_flag: Post names PDA's absence from DSM/ICD, but check that 'the direction matters' framing doesn't read as clinical endorsement of a contested label.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't no expectations. It's removing the threat around demands so connection is possible first. Expectations become workable from connection — not the other way around.
items.rationale: Gives PDA parents a quotable defense against 'you're just letting them do whatever.' The logic holds up in a conversation with a skeptical pediatrician or teacher.

items.text: The ADHD app graveyard is real. Complex productivity systems require executive function to maintain — often more than they save. The setup becomes its own avoidance task.
items.rationale: Names a widely shared ADHD experience with precision. 'The setup becomes its own avoidance task' is the kind of line people screenshot. The naming is the whole value here.

items.text: If your productivity system needs maintenance, it's too heavy. For ADHD brains, setup becomes procrastination. One list. One tool. Radical simplification usually wins.
items.rationale: Pairs with the micro-insight post but delivers the counter-move directly — concrete, actionable, nothing to download. The rhythm of the last three sentences is punchy and copy-paste-ready.

items.text: 72% of neurodivergent employees feel pressure to mask or perform neurotypicality at work. Not a fringe experience. A documented, systemic one. What would workplaces look like if that number dropped?
items.rationale: The stat transforms a private, isolating experience into a verifiable pattern. The closing question opens genuine conversation without demanding a particular answer or framing.

items.text: Demand avoidance isn't defiance. It's a threat response — the same fight/flight/freeze the nervous system runs on any perceived danger. That shifts the question from 'why won't you' to 'what do you need first?'
items.rationale: The pivot from moral failing to nervous-system wiring is the most validating move available for this topic. The question shift at the end is immediately usable by parents, teachers, and managers.

items.text: What does 'feeling safe' actually feel like for you — and did you have to learn it from scratch? For a lot of autistic adults, calm was so elusive for so long it stopped feeling like something that belonged to them.
items.rationale: Opens reflection without demanding vulnerability. Specific enough to feel real — not generic wellness content. The second sentence validates the experience without speaking for anyone.
items.sensitivity_flag: Polyvagal framing underpinning this angle has thin 2026 peer-reviewed anchors per briefing note. Post as written is evergreen enough to stand without citation, but avoid adding specific polyvagal claims in replies.
